proxy.tls.hintOff: Plain HTTP: no certificate is served for this hostname.
proxy.tls.hintManual: Serves the certificate pair uploaded below.
proxy.tls.hintEmpty: A public hostname gets an ACME certificate; a local-only name gets the engine’s own CA.
proxy.tls.hintPublic: A public hostname, so the engine asks a CA for a certificate — an ACME account e-mail is needed.
proxy.tls.hintLocal: A local-only name, so the engine signs it with its own locally-trusted CA.
proxy.engine.title: Engine
proxy.engine.description: The reverse proxy itself. The panel downloads the current build, supervises it and applies its configuration through the engine's own admin API.
proxy.engine.notInFrame: The proxy state is not in this panel's frame yet.
proxy.engine.readFailed: The engine could not be read
proxy.engine.installNote: Installing downloads the current {engine} release the panel supervises — about 46 MB, once. Nothing is exposed until a route is added and the proxy is switched on.
proxy.engine.setcapHint: A privileged port (below 1024) needs this once on Linux:
proxy.engine.revertHint: Go back to the configuration that applied before the last one
proxy.listener.title: Listener & certificates
proxy.listener.description: Where the proxy listens. 80 and 443 are what a router forwards and what an ACME challenge expects; a port below 1024 needs a privileged bind.
proxy.listener.runHint: Saved with Save settings; the panel starts or stops the engine to match.
proxy.listener.httpPortHint: ACME HTTP-01 challenges and the redirect to HTTPS.
proxy.listener.forwardHint: Running unprivileged — forward 80 and 443 to these ports on your router.
proxy.listener.privilegedTitle: A port below 1024 needs a privileged bind
proxy.listener.privilegedBody: Running the panel as your own user cannot bind 80 or 443 without permission. Either grant it once {how} and restart the engine, or keep {http}/{https} and forward 80/443 from your router. On Windows the port is free to bind, but something else may hold it.
proxy.listener.emailHint: Let's Encrypt uses it to warn you about an expiring certificate. A local-only name gets the engine's own CA and needs none.
proxy.listener.emailNeededTitle: An e-mail is needed for automatic HTTPS
proxy.listener.emailNeededBody: “{host}” is a public hostname, so the engine asks a CA for a certificate and the account address is required. Fill it in, switch the route's TLS off, or turn on the staging endpoint while you try things out.
proxy.listener.stagingHint: Untrusted certificates and no rate-limit burn while you try things out.
proxy.listener.dns01Hint: The panel writes the challenge record through a route's DNS account, so no inbound port is needed to get a certificate.
proxy.listener.resolversHint: Nameservers the engine reads the record from; empty uses its own. Needed where split-horizon DNS shows it a different view.
proxy.listener.noAccountTitle: No DNS account can answer a challenge
proxy.listener.noAccountBody: DNS-01 is on, but no account has credentials it can use. Add one under Workspace Settings → Dynamic DNS, or public names stay on the port challenges and wait for a CA that cannot reach them.
proxy.listener.manyAccountsTitle: Each public route has to pick an account
proxy.listener.manyAccountsBody: More than one account can answer, so “Automatic” cannot choose. Pick one per route, or those names stay on the port challenges.
proxy.listener.accountNote: Each route picks its own account, so names in different zones each get the right one. A route left on “Automatic” uses the only account the table names. A name no account answers stays on the port challenges.
proxy.listener.pendingNote: A public name whose certificate is still being issued is reachable in the meantime — over HTTPS with a temporary untrusted certificate, or over plain HTTP with a page naming the ports to forward.
proxy.routes.title: Routes
proxy.routes.description: One public hostname per service. A route may point at a supervised server in any workspace, at this panel, or at a literal upstream.
proxy.routes.cannotSaveTitle: These routes cannot be saved as they stand
proxy.routes.emptyDescription: Add one to expose a server through a domain — the engine gets the certificate on its own.
proxy.routeDialog.description: A hostname, what it forwards to, and how it is served over TLS.
proxy.routeDialog.localNote: A local-only name is signed by the engine's own CA, so no DNS account is involved.
proxy.routeDialog.stoppedNote: A server that is stopped is not routed: the row shows “No upstream” until it runs again.
proxy.routeDialog.upstreamHint: A literal address, including the port. A scheme is optional.
proxy.routeDialog.panelNote: Serving the control panel needs authentication on and a password that is not the default — the panel refuses the save otherwise.
proxy.account.automatic: Automatic (the only account that can answer)
proxy.account.gone: That account is no longer configured.
proxy.account.emptyHint: DNS-01 writes the challenge record here. Empty uses the only account that can answer a challenge, when there is one.
proxy.account.cannotWrite: A {provider} account cannot write TXT records, so it cannot answer a DNS-01 challenge.
proxy.account.noCredentialsYet: No credentials are stored for this {provider} account yet.
proxy.account.through: The challenge is written through this {provider} account.
proxy.certificate.title: Uploaded certificates
proxy.certificate.description: Served by routes set to “Uploaded certificate”. Everything else — public or local — is certified by the engine on its own.
proxy.certificate.emptyDescription: A route set to “Uploaded certificate” needs a pair covering its hostname, or the engine has nothing to serve for it.
proxy.certificate.subject: Subject
proxy.certificate.removeBody: The pair is deleted from disk. A route still set to “Uploaded certificate” keeps serving the engine's own certificate until you change it, and the panel refuses this while one still serves it.
proxy.certificateDialog.title: Add a certificate
proxy.certificateDialog.description: The pair is stored on disk under its id, and a route set to “Uploaded certificate” can serve it.
proxy.certificateDialog.label: Label
proxy.certificateDialog.errorId: the id must start with a letter or digit, then letters, digits, dash or underscore
proxy.certificateDialog.errorTaken: “{id}” is already used by another certificate
proxy.certificateDialog.errorPrivateKey: paste or choose the private key
proxy.retryButton.question: Ask the CA again for {host}?
proxy.retryButton.body: The engine failed to obtain a CA certificate for this hostname previously and is using its local CA. It retries automatically every {retryIn}.
proxy.retryButton.warning: Retrying now will kill this route and make it unavailable for a bit, are you sure to continue?
proxy.view.title: Reverse Proxy
proxy.view.description: Expose your servers through domains, with automatic HTTPS via 80/443 or a DNS challenge.
proxy.view.dnsNote: For DNS-01, add the domain's DNS provider to any workspace under Workspace Settings → Dynamic DNS; a route can then pick that account, from any workspace.
proxy.view.readFailed: The reverse proxy could not be read
proxy.validation.idPattern: the id must start with a letter or digit, then letters, digits, dash or underscore
proxy.validation.hostPattern: a hostname of letters, digits, dots and dashes, e.g. home.example.com
proxy.validation.hostTaken: "{host}" is already routed for this path
proxy.validation.pathSpace: a path prefix cannot contain a space
proxy.validation.workspaceRequired: pick the workspace that owns the server
proxy.validation.serverRequired: pick a server in that workspace
